chapter: The Lunceford years: Europe, rivals and bandsmen
title: Wilcox the tight-fisted pianist
summary: Crawford describes Wilcox as thrifty, conscientious and devoted to the band, contrasting Freddie Webster.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Well, that I didn't know, but I think they knew that he was colored. But he didn't look it. He was white as Dorsey. What I mean, not hairstyle, because he had always black hair. Good hair, like Cab Calloway. And after Willie, Wilcox, pianist. Wilcox was always a tight man. By that I mean he wasn't a spendthrift. He'd hold on to a dime or a nickel as long as he could. He wouldn't spend on nobody, like, buy a drink for some [broad,] no. He was a tight man. Good, conscientious player, and his whole body and soul was for that band, the same as Willie Smith and all the rest of the guys. They wouldn't be there if they found -- well, I
told you about Freddie Webster. Couldn't understand why we always made time. He didn't know we came up with the band that demanded you have to imagine that. Jimmy Lunceford --
